paras: The lynching at Bloomington, Illinois, was an act of mob violence known only from a passing reference in a Chicago Tribune editorial reprinted on December 2, 1881. The editorial named no victim, date or circumstances, and cited the episode, with a lynching at Durand, Wisconsin, as a sign that the public believed criminal justice had failed.

The editorial referred to "the lynching at Bloomington, Ill.," in the past tense, so the act took place some time before early December 1881. It attributed the act to "the mob at Bloomington" and said the mob's motto was that "the law is a farce." The piece did not say whether anyone was killed, who the victim was, or of what the victim was accused, and it mentioned no race.
No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution connected with the Bloomington lynching appears in the coverage.

The Tribune editorial, carried by The True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, used Bloomington and Durand to argue that lawyers and court procedure, rather than mobs, were the problem. It asked what such lynchings and the attempts upon the life of Guiteau were "if they are not symptoms of a profound and widespread conviction" that criminal justice was failing. Rather than condemning the mob, the writer said laymen could be excused for believing the law existed to keep great criminals from being punished, and claimed justice failed more often in Illinois and Wisconsin than in England or the Eastern states.

reader.title: Lynching at Bloomington, Illinois (1881)
bases: The only report, a reprinted Chicago Tribune editorial, calls the Bloomington episode 'the lynching at Bloomington, Ill.' and attributes it to a mob (A1).

A1 names a mob and a 'lynching' at Bloomington whose motto was that 'the law is a farce', which points to illegal action under a pretext of justice, but it gives no victim, no death and no size for the mob, so the standard definition cannot be applied.
One passing editorial reference (A1) is the only report; no news account of the Bloomington mob was found, and the Vance dispatches (A3, A4) concern a later threat at Minier.

set_aside: News brief on the coroner's verdict for Ed. Maxwell, lynched at Durand, Wis.; mentions a Bloomington, Ind., accident; nothing on a Bloomington, Ill., mob.
Bloomington dispatch of Dec. 2: George Vance arrested at 'Miner' accused of an outrage on a 10-year-old girl; 'thought the villian will be lynched'. A threat, after the editorial's date.
Bloomington dispatch of Dec. 6 on the Vance case at Minier, Tazewell County: 'not unlikely that he will be lynched to-night'. No killing reported.
Bloomington, Ill., dateline only for background on Ed. Maxwell, hanged by the mob at Durand, Wis.
